prompt: Which of these is a non-functional question about boxoffice?
hint: What it does, or how well it does it?

choices.text: Is a member charged 10% less than somebody without an account?
choices.why: That is about what it does: a functional question.

choices.text: Are six tickets accepted in one order, as R4 says?
choices.why: A rule about behaviour, so functional.

choices.text: How fast is booking with 200 people at once?
choices.why: Right: how fast, for how many, is how well.

choices.text: Can a used order still be refunded?
choices.why: A state rule, which lesson 5 tested as functional.

prompt: Match each family of testing to the question it asks.
hint: Ordinary use, the busiest day, past it, and for hours.

pairs.right: How quickly does it answer under ordinary use?
Does it still answer in time at the expected peak?
Where is the limit, and how does it fail there?
What goes wrong only after hours of ordinary load?

right_distractors: Is the price right for a student?

prompt: Which of these performance requirements can be tested?
hint: Could anyone say when it has failed?

choices.text: Pages must load quickly for nearly every visitor, at every hour of the day
choices.why: Quickly is a feeling; nobody can say when it failed.

choices.text: With 200 booking at once, 95% of pages answer within one second
choices.why: Right: a load, a share and a time, each one somebody's decision.

choices.text: The site must be fast
choices.why: It cannot fail, so it cannot pass.

choices.text: Performance must be acceptable to the theatre and to all of its customers
choices.why: Acceptable by what measure? The number is missing.

prompt: boxoffice's requirements say nothing about speed or load. What does this lesson ask a tester to do about it?
hint: A gap is a finding.

choices.text: Leave performance out, since nothing is required
choices.why: Silence in the requirements is a question to raise, not a permission.

choices.text: Choose a number herself and test against it
choices.why: Each number is a decision for the people who own the product.

choices.text: Load-test the theatre's live site to find the real number
choices.why: Never without permission, and a measurement is not a requirement.

choices.text: Raise the gap, and ask the client how fast and for how many
choices.why: Right: the question turns "fast" into something that can fail.

prompt: What does curl print with -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n'?
hint: The page itself is thrown away.

choices.text: The status code and the total time in seconds
choices.why: Right: 200 and a time, and nothing else.

choices.text: The page's HTML and its drawing time
choices.why: -o /dev/null throws the HTML away, and curl draws nothing.

choices.text: Every response header
choices.why: That is -D -, used in section 04.

choices.text: The version of the server
choices.why: The Server header carries that, and it is not asked for here.

prompt: In the lesson's run, the slowest of twenty requests sent together took 0.036099 seconds. About how many milliseconds is that?
hint: A thousand milliseconds in a second.

prompt: Ana times the home page at about two milliseconds on her laptop. What is wrong with reporting "boxoffice answers in 2 ms"?
hint: Who else was using it, and across what?

choices.text: curl cannot measure anything shorter than a second
choices.why: It printed 0.002166s; it measures fine.

choices.text: Times must be reported in seconds, not milliseconds
choices.why: The unit is a detail; the missing conditions are the problem.

choices.text: It leaves out the conditions it was taken in
choices.why: Right: one user, no network, a laptop. A measurement says something only about those.

choices.text: Two milliseconds is too fast to be a real result
choices.why: It is real, for one request on one machine talking to itself.

prompt: A load test reports that 95% of requests came in under 800 ms. What does that say about the other 5%?
hint: A percentile draws a line; it does not describe what is past it.

choices.text: They failed with errors
choices.why: Errors are counted separately; slow is not failed.

choices.text: They took 800 ms or more, and not how much more
choices.why: Right: the 5% past the line could be 801 ms or thirty seconds.

choices.text: They were dropped from the result as noise before it was computed
choices.why: They are in the result; the percentile is computed over all of them.

choices.text: Each of them took exactly 800 ms
choices.why: Nothing about the figure pins them to one value.

prompt: Match each load-testing tool to how its user scripts are written.
hint: One of the right-hand items is not a load tool at all.

pairs.right: Built in a graphical editor, in an older Java tool

right_distractors: Read aloud by a screen reader

prompt: A classmate suggests load-testing the theatre's real website to get realistic numbers. What does the lesson say?
hint: How does a load test look to the people running the servers?

choices.text: Fine, if it runs at night when nobody is booking and the servers are idle
choices.why: Night or day, it needs permission, and night may be when backups run.

choices.text: Fine, as long as it uses fewer than a hundred virtual users at a time
choices.why: The size is not the issue; permission is.

choices.text: Fine, because the site is public
choices.why: Public to visit is not permission to load.

choices.text: Not without permission: to its owners it looks like an attack
choices.why: Right: load tests run against an environment set aside, with the owners told.

prompt: What does boxoffice's traceback page disclose that a stranger should not see?
hint: Read it as a stranger would.

choices.text: The program's path and lines of its source code
choices.why: Right: free knowledge that saves somebody the guessing.

choices.text: The password of the seeded member account, in plain text
choices.why: No password appears in it.

choices.text: The list of every order placed so far
choices.why: It shows code, not data.

choices.text: Nothing: an error page is harmless
choices.why: It names the path, the language and the code.

prompt: Lesson 4 already reported the error page against R7. Why does this lesson file a second report about the same page?
hint: Who fixes each, and how urgently?

choices.text: Two reports about one page raise its priority in the tracker
choices.why: Duplicates do not raise priority; they waste triage time.

choices.text: The report about R7 was closed when version 1.1 shipped last week
choices.why: The release notes list it as known and not fixed.

choices.text: The leak is a different problem, for different people
choices.why: Right: R7 is about a sentence; disclosure is about what the page reveals.

choices.text: Security reports go straight to the client
choices.why: They go into the same tracker as any other report.

prompt: boxoffice accepts 12345678 as a password. How does the lesson treat that?
hint: Compare the program with R2.

choices.text: As a defect of the highest severity
choices.why: The program does what R2 says, so it is not a defect.

choices.text: As a question for the client about R2
choices.why: Right: the validation question of lesson 6, put with the evidence.

choices.text: As something to prove by breaking into an account
choices.why: No attacks: the observation is enough.

choices.text: As not worth mentioning, since R2 is met
choices.why: Meeting a weak rule is exactly what the client should hear about.

prompt: Why does HTTPS go into the plan as something to check in production, rather than into today's test run?
hint: Where does boxoffice run in this course?

choices.text: HTTPS is the developers' concern, not a tester's
choices.why: Checking the padlock and the redirect is squarely a tester's job.

choices.text: Plain http is acceptable for a theatre's sign-up page
choices.why: In production it would be a defect of the highest severity.

choices.text: Checking HTTPS requires an attack tool
choices.why: A browser's address bar is enough.

choices.text: The lab has no HTTPS to look at
choices.why: Right: boxoffice serves plain http on 127.0.0.1, so the check waits in the plan.

prompt: Signing up with member@example.org answers "There is already an account with that e-mail." What does the tester do with it?
hint: Helpful, and it tells a stranger something.

choices.text: Put the trade-off to the client
choices.why: Right: with the exact message, since whether it is acceptable depends on the business.

choices.text: Report it as a critical defect
choices.why: It meets the requirements; it is a choice with a cost.

choices.text: Rewrite the message in the code
choices.why: Testers report; they do not change the product.

choices.text: Nothing: the message is helpful, so it is fine
choices.why: Helpful and revealing at once is the point.

prompt: The best-known list of the commonest web security problems is the OWASP Top ___.
hint: A round number.

prompt: On the booking page, put the controls in the order Tab reaches them.
hint: Top to bottom, as the page reads.
trap: The button comes after everything it submits.

prompt: Why is the placeholder "Tickets (1 to 6)" not enough as the field's label?
hint: Type a 2 into the field and look again.

choices.text: HTML does not allow a placeholder on an input that also has a name
choices.why: It does; the problem is using it as the only label.

choices.text: Grey text fails every contrast rule, so the words cannot be read
choices.why: Contrast is a separate check; the label problem stands even in black.

choices.text: It vanishes once you type, and screen readers treat it unevenly
choices.why: Right: and clicking the words does not focus the field either.

choices.text: A placeholder makes the field required
choices.why: It has nothing to do with whether the field is required.

prompt: axe reports no violations on the booking page, with the WCAG 2.2 AA rules. What does that establish?
hint: What can a tool decide from markup?

choices.text: That the page meets WCAG 2.2 AA
choices.why: This very page has a field a person cannot use well, and axe passed it.

choices.text: Only that nothing axe can decide from the markup failed
choices.why: Right: whether a person can use the page is not decidable from markup.

choices.text: That the tickets field has a proper label
choices.why: axe counted the placeholder as a name; the field still has no label.

choices.text: That the keyboard walk can be skipped for this release and the next
choices.why: The walk found what the tool did not.

prompt: During the keyboard walk, focus goes into a date picker and Tab, Shift+Tab and Escape all leave it there. What has the tester found?
hint: Can you get out?

choices.text: A missing label on the date field
choices.why: A label is about naming the field, not leaving it.

choices.text: A focus outline that has been removed
choices.why: You could see where you were; you just could not leave.

choices.text: A problem only for screen reader users
choices.why: Anybody on a keyboard is stuck, sighted or not.

choices.text: A keyboard trap
choices.why: Right: it ends the session for anyone using the keyboard.

prompt: Match each finding to the family of testing it belongs to.
hint: One family on the right has none of these findings.

pairs.left: Booking takes nine seconds when 300 people book at once
An error page shows the program's path
The tickets field has no label
The table of shows scrolls sideways on a phone

prompt: Which report of slowness is the most useful to a developer?
hint: Could someone check it, and compare it with the next build?

choices.text: Booking is really slow today, much worse than it was last week, and customers are complaining
choices.why: Slow and worse are feelings; nothing here can be checked.

choices.text: The site feels sluggish on my machine
choices.why: Which page, how slow, which build?

choices.text: Booking Hamlet took 4.2 s in 3 of 5 tries, build 1.1, test environment, 10:15
choices.why: Right: a number, a page, a build, a place and a time.

choices.text: Performance does not meet expectations
choices.why: Whose expectations? There is not even a requirement to compare with.

prompt: Which of these did this lesson find on boxoffice with nothing but a browser, curl and the keyboard? Choose all that apply.
hint: No load tool, no scanner, no screen reader.

choices.text: The traceback that shows the program's path
choices.why: Yes: one curl, read as a stranger would.

choices.text: The Python version in the Server header
choices.why: Yes: curl -D - printed it.

choices.text: The tickets field with no label
choices.why: Yes: the markup, read with grep.

choices.text: The point where boxoffice fails under load
choices.why: No load test was run; the twenty requests only showed the shape.

choices.text: A password stolen from the outbox
choices.why: The check found the password nowhere in the outbox.
